worse.name: Bass Strait and Tasman Sea
worse.why: Colonial-era coastal traders lost between Sydney, Hobart, Launceston and Port Phillip, in a strait swept by westerly gales and strewn with islands and reefs; one section of the Wikipedia list carefully gathers these Australian losses, and receivers pick up relatively little AIS traffic here today.

worse.name: Rest of Lake Michigan
worse.why: Nineteenth- and early twentieth-century lake freighters and schooners caught by sudden autumn gales on a long, open lake, when lake traffic was far busier than it is today; the losses are richly documented by American newspapers and enthusiasts.

worse.name: Rest of the Great Lakes
worse.why: Lake Superior and Lake Huron storms, above all the November gales, which sank freighters that left no trace; busy lake trade a century ago.

worse.name: US Atlantic coast
worse.why: Cape Hatteras and the Diamond Shoals, Gulf Stream storms, and a long tail of American light aircraft and yachts, reported by an English-language press that Wikipedia draws on heavily.

worse.name: Caribbean Sea
worse.why: Hurricanes, and the warships and packets of the 1700s and 1800s (USS Insurgent, USS Albany, HMS Babet), plus light aircraft in recent decades.

worse.name: English Channel
worse.why: Pioneer aviators (Walter Powell, Cecil Grace, Gustav Hamel), pilots of the Battle of Britain, and Glenn Miller's aircraft: short flights over water, often in war, all well reported in English.

worse.name: Newfoundland and the Grand Banks
worse.why: Fog, ice and gales at the corner of the North Atlantic, where the great-circle routes to Europe begin: pioneer transatlantic flights of 1927 and 1928 and steamers such as the Arctic were lost here.
